newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia needs to reduce wage growth - economists.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia needs to reduce wage growth - economists.

text.p: Restricting wage rises in order to improve international competitiveness will be one of the most pressing tasks of Slovenia's new government next year, economists said on Monday.

"No matter who the new premier is, I think all parties realise the new government will have to have a more restrictive wage policy, limiting wage growth to about 3.5 percent next year," said Igor Strmsnik of the government-sponsored Institute of Macroeconomic Analysis and Development.
A general election last month brought an inconclusive result, giving neither left nor right a clear mandate. President Milan Kucan has to name a new candidate for prime minister by January 3.

"The growth of salaries is diminishing the international competitiveness of our economy and ... has to be pushed below the GDP growth," Samo Hribar Milic, project manager of the Slovenian Chamber of Economy, told Reuters.

Slovenia has the highest standard of living among the former communist countries. It signed an association agreement with the European Union in June and hopes to become a full member by the year 2001.
Milic said the chamber believed salary growth in 1997 should be at least two percentage points lower than GDP growth, which is expected to reach four percent next year.
In October the average gross salary was 135,595 tolars ($968), 21.1 percent higher than the 1995 average. GDP growth is projected at 3.5 percent this year.
"We will demand that the new government reduces social security payments and taxes on salaries and enforces tougher tax controls," Milic said.
In 1996 the government reduced social security payments to 38 percent of the gross salary from 44.7 percent but introduced a new tax on wages of up to six percent that varies according to salary.

The government also agreed to higher pay in many public sector areas this year after television and radio journalists, doctors and dentists, railway workers, air-traffic controllers and teachers all staged strikes.
"The government was the weakest in the area of salaries," Strmsnik said, tracing the trend to high wage expectations.
"When Slovenians think of Europe they think of European salaries and not of conditions that have to be fulfilled to get there," Strmsnik added. -- Ljubljana newsroom, 386-61-125-8439
